Area of Operations
An operational area defined by a commander for land and maritime forces that is large enough to accomplish missions and protect forces.<SEP>An area of operations is an operational area defined by a commander for land and maritime forces that should be large enough to accomplish missions and protect forces.<SEP>An Area of Operations is a geographical area assigned to a commander who holds responsibility for recovering isolated persons within its bounds.

Isolated Personnel
Personnel who are separated from their unit due to enemy action, disorientation, or environmental conditions and require recovery.<SEP>Isolated Personnel are individuals separated from their unit or friendly control due to enemy action, disorientation, or environmental conditions.

Army Personnel Recovery
Army Personnel Recovery involves military efforts taken to prepare for and execute the recovery and reintegration of isolated personnel.

Commander
An individual who defines operational areas, assigns areas of operations to subordinates, and manages terrain and fires.<SEP>The individual responsible for conducting operations, clearing fires, and ensuring security within an assigned area.<SEP>A commander is an individual responsible for synchronizing combat power, defining areas of operations, and managing areas of influence.<SEP>The Commander is the individual assigned an Area of Operations (AO) responsible for recovering and returning isolated persons to friendly control.<SEP>An individual responsible for employing forces, designating engagement areas, and directing operations to achieve positional advantages.<SEP>A leader who assumes risk, task-organizes capabilities, and weights the decisive operation to accomplish the mission.

Airspace Element
The Airspace Element is the functional lead for the division staff, responsible for integrating airspace operations and developing standard operating procedures.

Airspace Control
Airspace Control consists of capabilities and procedures used to increase operational effectiveness by promoting the safe, efficient, and flexible use of airspace.

Deliberate Recovery
Deliberate Recovery is a planned operation conducted when immediate recovery is not undertaken or is unsuccessful.

Division Joint Air-Ground Integration Center
The Division Joint Air-Ground Integration Center (JAGIC) is an organization composed of the Army's fires cell, air missile defense cell, airspace element, and USAF's air support operations center and tactical air control party.

Immediate Recovery
Immediate Recovery is a response triggered without detailed planning in the event of isolation, requiring analysis of mission variables.

Air Support Operations Center
The Air Support Operations Center (ASOC) is a United States Air Force unit co-located with the division headquarters to command and control air operations.<SEP>An organization that provides an effective means to coordinate suppression of enemy air defense in division-assigned airspace.

Tactical Air Control Party
The Tactical Air Control Party is a unit co-located with the division headquarters and part of the airspace control working group.

Airspace Control Authority
The Airspace Control Authority is the entity responsible for assigning a volume of airspace to the division headquarters.<SEP>The authority responsible for delegating the control of airspace to a division in accordance with plans and orders.

Theater Airspace Control Plan
The Theater Airspace Control Plan is a document that the airspace element plans and updates with input to ensure consistency with joint procedures.

FM 3-50
FM 3-50 is a field manual providing information on Army personnel recovery and the operations process.

United States Air Force
The United States Air Force aligns air support operations center capabilities with Army divisions.<SEP>The military service branch that operates air support operations centers.

JP 3-52
JP 3-52 is a joint publication defining airspace control capabilities and procedures.<SEP>A joint publication that provides the definition for coordinating altitude and coordination level.

Airspace Control Working Group
The Airspace Control Working Group integrates airspace operations with functional and integrating cells.

Air Missile Defense Cell
The Air Missile Defense Cell is a component of the division joint air-ground integration center (JAGIC).

Fires Cell
The Fires Cell is a component of the division joint air-ground integration center (JAGIC).

Joint Task Force Components
Joint Task Force Components are supported by Army forces during external supported recovery operations.

Interagency Organizations
Interagency Organizations are supported by Army forces during external supported recovery operations.

Multinational Forces
Multinational Forces receive airspace control support from the division headquarters and are supported during recovery operations.<SEP>Forces with whom the special operations command–forward synchronizes efforts.

Army Battlefield Coordination Detachment
The Army Battlefield Coordination Detachment coordinates with the division airspace element through its airspace section.

Airspace Control Order
An order implementing the airspace control plan.<SEP>An Airspace Control Order is a document into which airspace requirements are integrated.<SEP>A document into which special operations requests are coordinated by the special operations liaison element.

Close Air Support
Close Air Support is an operation commanded and controlled by the Air Support Operations Center.

Brigade
A Brigade is a subordinate unit to which the division headquarters may delegate airspace management responsibilities.<SEP>An Army echelon higher than a battalion and part of a division.<SEP>A unit consisting of two or more battalions and a headquarters company or detachment, normally containing 2,500 to 5,000 Soldiers.

Meeting Engagement
A combat action that occurs when a moving force, incompletely deployed for battle, engages an enemy at an unexpected time and place.<SEP>A combat action that occurs when a force makes unexpected contact with an enemy or when opponents are aware of each other and decide to attack.

Suppression of Enemy Air Defense
A military operation coordinated by air support operations centers within division-assigned airspace.<SEP>Suppression of Enemy Air Defense is an operation coordinated by the Air Support Operations Center within division-assigned airspace.

Maneuver
The employment of forces through movement in combination with fires and information to achieve a position of advantage.<SEP>A tactical action enabled by movement, used to obtain positional advantage over an enemy.<SEP>A principle of war closely associated with the concept of weighting the decisive operation.

ATP 3-92
ATP 3-92 is a publication containing information on the airspace element's responsibilities when the division is an operational headquarters.

ATP 3-91.1
A publication containing descriptions of functions related to requesting authority to control division-assigned airspace.<SEP>ATP 3-91.1 describes functions regarding the request for authority to control division-assigned airspace.

Reconnaissance
The active collection of information, usually including human participation, that produces combat information.<SEP>A mission undertaken to obtain information, the ineffectiveness of which often leads to meeting engagements.<SEP>A method used to gather information; its ineffectiveness can lead to unexpected contact and meeting engagements.

Initiative
A strategic imperative in combat where a force acts first to gain an advantage, often seized through prompt execution of battle drills.

Battle Drills
Rehearsed and well-understood actions made in response to common battlefield occurrences, requiring a "go" order instead of a plan.

Movement
The positioning of combat power to establish conditions for maneuver, directed through techniques and formations.

Supporting Range
The distance one unit can be separated from another while remaining within the maximum range of its weapons systems.<SEP>One of two aspects of mutual support, referring to the ability to support with direct or indirect fires.

Mutual Support
Support that units render each other against an enemy based on assigned tasks, relative position, and inherent capabilities.

Supporting Distance
The distance between two units that allows one to aid the other in time to prevent defeat or regain control.<SEP>One of two aspects of mutual support, equaling supporting range when friendly forces are static.

Deep Areas
Areas designated by commanders within their AO to describe the physical arrangement of forces.

Operation
A sequence of tactical actions with a common purpose, including planning, preparing, executing, and assessing offensive, defensive, and stability tasks.

Operational Framework
A cognitive tool used to assist commanders in visualizing and describing the application of combat power in time, space, purpose, and resources.

Close Areas
Areas designated by commanders within their AO as part of the operational framework's physical arrangement.

AO (Area of Operations)
An area assigned to a commander for the conduct of operations, serving as a component of the operational framework.

Piecemeal Commitment
The immediate employment of units in combat as they become available, often unsynchronized, which risks defeat in detail.

Consolidation Areas
Areas designated by commanders within their AO to describe the physical arrangement of forces in time, space, and purpose.

Support Areas
Areas designated by commanders within their AO to facilitate operations.

Decisive Operations
Operations established by commanders to articulate the purpose of an operation, directly leading to mission accomplishment.

Sustaining Operations
Operations established by commanders to enable decisive and shaping operations.

Shaping Operations
Shaping Operations are secondary efforts where minimum essential combat power is expended to support the decisive operation.<SEP>Operations where commanders expend minimum essential combat power to support the decisive operation.<SEP>Operations established by commanders to create conditions for decisive operations.<SEP>Operations conducted by a division headquarters to create favorable conditions for the success of subordinate units.<SEP>Operations conducted by a division headquarters within its area of operations to create favorable conditions.

Defeat in Detail
A technique of concentrating overwhelming combat power against separate parts of a force rather than defeating the entire force at once.<SEP>The destruction of smaller committed forces, a risk associated with piecemeal commitment.

Reorganization
A component of reconstitution possible at the tactical level to restore a unit.

Commanders
Leaders who perform enabling operations, consider mission variables, and use warfighting functions to accomplish missions.<SEP>Individuals responsible for integrating environmental considerations, planning operations, requesting resources, and balancing stability tasks with combat operations.<SEP>Individuals responsible for performing reconstitution, constituting reserves, and adhering to rules of engagement.<SEP>Leaders responsible for visualizing operations, assigning areas, and implementing reconstitution.

Movement Formations
Formations used by Army forces to direct movement and establish conditions for maneuver.

Reconstitution
A total process performed by commanders to raise combat effectiveness, involving tasks like removing units from combat and reestablishing cohesion.<SEP>Actions planned and implemented by commanders to restore units to a desired level of combat effectiveness, including regeneration and reorganization.

Defense
One of the four elements of decisive action involving defensive operations.<SEP>A type of military operation where commanders select tactical positions to achieve maximum mutual support.

Regeneration
A process at the tactical level that requires support from higher echelons to restore units.<SEP>A component of reconstitution that requires support from higher echelons to restore a unit.

Movement Techniques
Techniques used by Army forces to direct movement and mitigate the risk of unexpected enemy contact.

Enabling Operations
Operations performed by commanders to help in the planning, preparation, and execution of decisive action elements.<SEP>Operations included in the sequence of tactical actions to support the achievement of objectives.

Direct Fires
Fire delivered directly at the enemy, utilized by units to support each other and prevent enemy engagement.

Indirect Fires
Fire delivered at a target not visible to the firer, utilized by units to provide mutual support.

Infiltration
A form of maneuver involving movement by small groups through enemy positions.<SEP>An enemy action characterized by covert movement into an area, which mutual support helps to prevent.

Offense
One of the four elements of decisive action involving offensive operations.<SEP>A type of military operation where commanders maneuver subordinate forces to ensure mutual support.

Momentum
A tactical quality that piecemeal commitment may be advantageous to maintain.

Stability Operations
A category of operations included within the scope of an operation, focused on maintaining order.

Main Effort
A focus of operations where the commander concentrates combat power to achieve results.<SEP>A designation by commanders to prioritize the shifting of resources within the operational framework.<SEP>A tactical concept that can be weighted by commanders, often closely associated with the decisive operation.

Divisions
Tactical units employed by a corps to achieve objectives on land, typically numbering two to five under a corps.

Multi-functional Brigades
Brigades employed by a corps or field army to achieve objectives on land.<SEP>A type of brigade employed by a division to achieve objectives on land.

Supporting Effort
A designation by commanders to support the prioritization of resources within the operational framework.

Mass
The concentration of combat power, which piecemeal commitment fails to ensure.<SEP>A principle of war closely associated with the concept of weighting the decisive operation.

Division Headquarters
A division headquarters leverages joint force capabilities, conducts shaping operations, allocates resources, designates efforts, and establishes priorities for subordinate units.<SEP>A self-contained organization with a command group and a fully functional staff that BCTs synchronize plans and actions for to accomplish tasks.

Subordinate Units
Units that cooperate to accomplish a mission as directed by the concept of operations.<SEP>Military units that may become combat ineffective and require reconstitution.<SEP>Units that operate under a division headquarters, receiving resources and support priorities to achieve success.

Corps
A higher echelon headquarters that can integrate functional brigade airspace requirements and task multifunctional support brigades.<SEP>The highest Army echelon mentioned, consisting of divisions.<SEP>A corps is an echelon of command and tactical formation that employs divisions and brigades to achieve objectives on land, exercising operational control over Army divisions.<SEP>A Corps receives complementary effects supporting freedom of action from special operations joint task forces.<SEP>Corps is a military unit level that requires a Psychological Operations group for command and control capabilities.

Joint Force Land Component Command
An operational-level command role that a field army or corps may serve as, requiring augmentation from joint and multinational forces.

Functional Brigades
Brigades employed by a corps or field army to achieve objectives on land, providing specific functional support.<SEP>A type of brigade employed by a division to achieve objectives on land.

Theater Army
An organization that provides capabilities and units to a corps for conducting operations.<SEP>The theater army provides resources to support and sustain Special Forces long-term operations in established combat theaters.

Large-scale Combat Operations
Large-scale combat operations are a type of military operation where units performing close combat are unlikely to conduct stability tasks.<SEP>High-intensity operations that require specific considerations for personnel recovery.<SEP>Operations that may require a corps headquarters to function as a tactical land headquarters or the establishment of a field army.

Marine Corps Units
Units over which a corps exercises tactical control.

Multinational Units
Units over which a corps exercises tactical control.

Corps Commander
The individual responsible for determining appropriate command and support relationships for subordinate divisions and brigades within a corps.

Field Army
A field army is an echelon of command that employs multiple corps and brigades, serving as the senior tactical or operational-level command.

ARFOR
Army Forces; a role served by the field army for multi-corps operations.<SEP>The Army component and senior Army headquarters of all Army forces assigned or attached to a combatant command.

AO
The Area of Operations where a division headquarters conducts shaping operations to create favorable conditions.

Peer and Near-peer Adversaries
Adversaries capable of conducting large-scale ground combat, influencing the deployment of field armies.

Area of Responsibility
The geographic area assigned to a field army, tailored by the Army to prevailing conditions.

Combat Aviation Brigade
A unit generally required by a corps to conduct large-scale combat operations.<SEP>A unit assigned to a division conducting large-scale ground combat operations.<SEP>A type of multifunctional support brigade.

Expeditionary Sustainment Command
A unit generally required by a corps to conduct large-scale combat operations.

Field Artillery Brigade
A unit required by a corps for large-scale combat operations, generally not retained in reserve.

Joint Combat Support Agencies
Agencies that provide support to a corps alongside theater military intelligence and signal organizations.

Maneuver Enhancement Brigade
A type of unit whose organizational design allows it to be assigned an area of operations, similar to a Brigade Combat Team.<SEP>A brigade capable of and responsible for airspace management of Army airspace users within their area of operations.<SEP>A unit generally required by a corps to conduct large-scale combat operations.<SEP>A unit assigned to a division conducting large-scale ground combat operations.<SEP>A type of multifunctional support brigade.

Company
A military unit subdivided into platoons.<SEP>A unit consisting of two or more platoons, usually of the same type, with a headquarters and a limited capacity for self-support.<SEP>A unit that can be attached to or detached from Brigade Combat Teams or their organic battalions.

Consolidation of Gains Activities
Activities for which field artillery brigades are not used, unlike other brigades that may be retained for this purpose.

Theater Military Intelligence Brigade
A brigade required by a corps to conduct large-scale combat operations.

The Army
The overarching organization that tailors each field army to the conditions prevailing in its assigned area of responsibility.

Detachment
A tactical element organized on either a temporary or permanent basis for special duties.

Troop
A type of military unit equivalent to a company.<SEP>A company-size unit in a cavalry organization.

Platoon
A subdivision of a company consisting of two or more squads or sections, normally led by a lieutenant.<SEP>A subdivision of a company or troop consisting of two or more squads or sections, normally led by a lieutenant.

Functional Units
Units including military police, engineer, air and missile defense, and military intelligence that operate in command or support relationships with a division.

Battery
A type of military unit equivalent to a company.<SEP>A company-size unit in a field artillery or air defense artillery battalion.

Lieutenant
A rank that normally leads a platoon.<SEP>A person who normally leads a platoon.

Battalion
An Army echelon higher than a company and part of a brigade.<SEP>A unit consisting of two or more company-, battery-, or troop-size units and a headquarters, typically ranging from 500 to 800 Soldiers.

Squadron
A unit echelon in cavalry organizations equivalent to a battalion.

Regiment
A higher echelon unit than a battalion.

Group
A higher echelon unit than a battalion.

Brigade Combat Team
A type of maneuver unit to which commanders normally assign areas of operations.<SEP>A combined arms organization consisting of a brigade headquarters, at least two maneuver battalions, and necessary supporting functional capabilities.<SEP>A combined arms organization consisting of a brigade headquarters, at least two maneuver battalions, and necessary supporting functional capabilities, serving as the largest fixed tactical units in the Army.<SEP>A military unit typically supported by a Civil Affairs company during deployment.<SEP>A Brigade Combat Team receives complementary effects supporting freedom of action from special operations joint task forces.

Company Team
A combined arms organization formed by attaching one or more nonorganic platoons to a company.

Task Force
A maneuver battalion-size unit formed by task-organizing subordinate maneuver battalions with support companies.

Cavalry
An organization type where companies are referred to as troops and battalions as squadrons.

Squad
A small military unit typically containing two or more fire teams, usually led by a staff sergeant.<SEP>A subunit that forms part of a platoon.

Section
A tactical unit smaller than a platoon and larger than a squad, used by the Army and Marine Corps.<SEP>A subunit that forms part of a platoon or a tactical element like a tank section.

Headquarters
A command element within a company, battalion, or brigade.<SEP>An element of the Special Operations Joint Task Force that provides command and control of all forces in the task force.

Field Artillery
A branch of the Army where companies are referred to as batteries.

Air Defense Artillery
A branch of the Army where companies are referred to as batteries.

Soldiers
Personnel who constitute the manpower of Army units such as platoons and companies.<SEP>Individuals affiliated with a regiment for whom history, espirit de corps, and traditions are perpetuated.<SEP>Soldiers are affected by the effects of battle along with units, leaders, and equipment during extended operations.

Maneuver Battalion
A battalion containing a headquarters company and branch-specific line companies.<SEP>A unit component of a Brigade Combat Team, with at least two normally contained in a BCT.

Sustainment Battalion
A type of battalion that performs functional services and is often larger than standard battalions.

Fire Team
A small military unit typically containing four or fewer Soldiers, capable of autonomous operations.<SEP>A small tactical unit mentioned as an example of a component within Army systems.

Tank Section
A tactical unit mentioned as an example of a component within Army systems.

Headquarters Company
A company that serves as the command element for maneuver battalions and brigades.

Headquarters Detachment
A detachment serving as the command element for non-maneuver battalions.

Special Forces Company
A type of company that has subordinate detachments instead of platoons, organized for independent operations.<SEP>Composed of a company headquarters (Special Forces operational detachment–bravo) and six Special Forces operational detachments–alpha.<SEP>May establish a small temporary base within a joint operational area.

Engineers
Supporting units that can be included in company teams as squads or platoons.

BCT Commander
A commander who can task-organize subordinate maneuver battalions to form task forces.

Armor Company
A type of company found in combined arms battalions or used to form company teams.

Mechanized Infantry Company
A type of company found in combined arms battalions or used to form company teams.

Combined Arms Battalion
A type of battalion containing a mix of mechanized infantry and armor companies in addition to a headquarters company.

Engineer Battalion
A type of battalion that can be reinforced to form engineer task forces.

Division Commander
A commander who utilizes BCTs and various brigades to accomplish missions.

Non-maneuver Battalion
A type of battalion that typically has a headquarters detachment instead of a headquarters company.

Infantry BCT
A type of Brigade Combat Team used by division commanders.

Field Artillery Battalion
A unit normally contained in all types of Brigade Combat Teams.<SEP>A type of battalion that controls batteries and may control batteries from other field artillery battalions.

Engineer Company
A type of company used to reinforce engineer battalions.

Engineer Task Force
A task force formed by reinforcing an engineer battalion with engineer companies and platoons.

Functional Brigade
A brigade that may fall under the tactical or operational control of a BCT, maneuver enhancement brigade, corps, or division.<SEP>A type of brigade that performs specific functions, such as air and missile defense or military police.

Armored BCT
A type of Brigade Combat Team used by division commanders.

Stryker BCT
A type of Brigade Combat Team used by division commanders.

Multifunctional Support Brigade
A type of brigade that supports division commanders, including field artillery and sustainment brigades.

Sustainment Brigade
A unit assigned to a division conducting large-scale ground combat operations.<SEP>A type of multifunctional support brigade.<SEP>A brigade included within the 1st Special Forces Command structure.

Air And Missile Defense Brigade
A type of functional brigade.

Civil Affairs Brigade
A type of functional brigade.<SEP>Includes Reserve and Active Component brigades assigned to support special operations commanders.<SEP>A deployable unit providing global, regional, and country-focused Civil Affairs capabilities to commanders.

Engineer Brigade
A type of functional brigade.

Military Police Brigade
A type of functional brigade.

Brigade Task Force
A unit formed when a brigade or BCT task-organizes by attachment or detachment of outside organizations.

Army
The Army is the military service to which the described units and organizations belong, operating as a military organization with echelons ranging from fire teams to corps. As a military branch, it retains two tactical regiments and organizes division headquarters staff. In 2008, The Army established six warfighting functions that linked to joint functions. The Army serves as the military branch context for sustainment brigades and special operations forces, notably containing the largest number of special operations units within the Department of Defense. It functions as a higher-echelon service under whose operational control special operations task forces may operate.

Regarding specific capabilities, The Army contains the 95th Civil Affairs Brigade and utilizes Civil Affairs capabilities for missions. It also utilizes Psychological Operations units and special operations regiments for various military missions. For planning and modeling purposes, The Army uses rules of allocation to model force composition and employs special operations forces in wargaming scenarios.

Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
Tasks performed by commanders within their areas of operations to maintain current and accurate common operational pictures.

Terrain Management
The process of allocating terrain by establishing areas of operations, designating assembly areas, and specifying locations for units to deconflict activities.

Intelligence Process
A model consisting of four steps and two continuing activities that describes how the intelligence warfighting function facilitates situational understanding.

Intelligence Operations
Tasks undertaken by military intelligence units through intelligence disciplines to obtain information to satisfy validated requirements.

ADP 3-90
A publication titled Common Tactical Concepts and Echelons published on 31 July 2019.<SEP>ADP 3-90 is an Army Doctrine Publication dated 31 July 2019, discussing common tactical concepts and echelons.

Information Collection
A responsibility within an area of operations involving intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance to maintain a common operational picture.

Surveillance
A systematic, continuous collection of information involving active and passive activities that produces combat information.

Security Operations
Operations performed by commanders to provide early warning of enemy operations and time for forces to react.<SEP>Operations performed by commanders to provide early warning of enemy operations, time and maneuver space for reaction, and protection for forces.

Common Operational Picture
A current and accurate representation of the area of operations shared with higher echelon, adjacent, subordinate, and tenant units.

Intelligence Disciplines
Specific fields of intelligence collection, including counterintelligence, geospatial intelligence, and human intelligence, among others.

Combat Information
Information produced by surveillance and reconnaissance that meets one or more of the commander’s critical information requirements.

Uncommitted Forces
Forces not in contact with an enemy or deployed on a specific mission, used to exploit success or avoid failure.<SEP>Forces used by commanders to exploit success or avoid failure, exemplified by echelon reserves.

Echelon Reserves
A specific type of uncommitted force held back from the main effort to be used when needed.

Commander's Critical Information Requirements
Critical information requirements that combat information is intended to meet or satisfy.

Enemy
The opposing force or threat whose operations, actions, and terrain are the focus of reconnaissance and security measures.<SEP>The opposing force or threat against which security operations provide early and accurate warning.<SEP>The opposing force or adversary against which friendly forces employ maneuver, fires, and defeat mechanisms.<SEP>The opposing force relative to friendly units, used as a reference for tactical mobility and supporting distance.

Higher Echelon Headquarters
A headquarters that imposes control measures within a subordinate unit's area of operations.

Decisive Operation
The Decisive Operation is the primary effort where maximum possible combat power is allocated through economy of force.<SEP>The operation that directly accomplishes the mission.<SEP>The main operation that receives the maximum possible combat power generated by economy of force measures.<SEP>The operation that directly accomplishes the mission and is the focus of the commander's efforts.

Forms of Maneuver
Tactical concepts covered in the chapter, related to offensive operations.<SEP>Distinct tactical combinations of fire and movement, including envelopment, frontal assault, infiltration, penetration, and turning movement.

Envelopment
A form of maneuver where forces bypass the enemy's front to strike at their flanks or rear.

Frontal Assault
A form of maneuver where forces attack along the enemy's front.

Penetration
A form of maneuver used to break through enemy lines.

Turning Movement
A form of maneuver designed to force the enemy to abandon their position.

Forms of Defense
Tactical concepts covered in the chapter, related to defensive operations.<SEP>Defensive arrangements including perimeter defense, defense of a linear obstacle, and reverse slope defense.

Crew
A small military unit consisting of all personnel operating a particular system, such as a mortar or tank.

Reverse Slope Defense
A form of defense conducted on the slope of a hill or ridge that is hidden from enemy observation.

Perimeter Defense
A form of defense oriented in all directions to protect a specific location.

Defense of a Linear Obstacle
A form of defense conducted along a specific terrain feature or boundary.

Marine Corps
A military organization that utilizes the section unit structure alongside the Army.

Task Organization
The process of organizing available capabilities to accomplish the mission and generate combined arms effects.

Division
A military unit responsible for controlling assigned airspace and integrating airspace use between brigades.<SEP>An Army echelon higher than a brigade and part of a corps.<SEP>An echelon of command and tactical formation that employs brigade combat teams and brigades to achieve objectives on land.<SEP>A Division receives complementary effects supporting freedom of action from special operations joint task forces.

Staff Sergeant
A rank that usually leads a squad.

Course of Action
A potential plan (COA) elaborated using forms of maneuver and defense, upon which a commander builds a scheme.

Soldier
An individual member of the Army who comprises units such as fire teams and squads.<SEP>Individuals who are assessed, selected, educated, and trained by the JFK Special Warfare Center to join the operational force.

Mortar
A type of weapons system operated by a crew.

Tank
A vehicle system operated by a crew.

Leader
An individual who uses forms of maneuver and forms of defense to elaborate courses of action and schemes of maneuver.

Sergeant
A rank that usually leads a fire team.

ADP 5-0
A publication referenced for the definition and additional information on the concept of operations.<SEP>A reference document that discusses command and support relationships.

Machinegun
A type of weapons system operated by a crew.

Target Acquisition Radar
A sensor system operated by a crew for identifying targets.

FM 3-90-1
A field manual containing detailed information on individual tactical mission tasks.<SEP>A field manual that provides a discussion of the forms of maneuver.

ADP 3-0
An Army doctrinal publication referenced for information on operational variables, mission variables, and warfighting functions.<SEP>ADP 3-0 is a doctrinal publication referenced for definitions regarding warfighting functions and defeat mechanisms.<SEP>A publication mentioning responsibilities associated with a unit assigned an area of operations, excluding environmental issues.<SEP>An Army doctrine publication referenced as the source for the definition of position of relative advantage.<SEP>A reference document that defines the decisive operation.

Static Force
A unit that conducts a defense of a linear obstacle during a mobile defense.

Simultaneity
A key component of understanding decisive action and the use of forms of maneuver and defense.

Striking Force
A unit that executes an envelopment during a mobile defense.

Noncommissioned Officer
A rank category that includes the senior crewmember for certain systems.

Commissioned Officer
A rank category that can include the senior crewmember for certain systems.

Common Tactical Concepts
Concepts applied by tacticians alongside military definitions and echelons during offensive and defensive operations.

Warrant Officer
A rank category that can include the senior crewmember for certain systems.

Echelons
Tactical echelons and organizations used by tacticians to conduct operations.

Joint Interdependence
The purposeful reliance by one Service on another Service to complement and reinforce each other's effects.

Principles of Joint Operations
Twelve principles originating from Army doctrine that provide general guidance for conducting military operations and link theory to application.

Army Forces
Military forces that conduct offensive and defensive operations as members of an interdependent joint force.

Operational Variables
Eight interrelated aspects (political, military, economic, social, information, infrastructure, physical environment, and time) used to describe an operational environment.

Army Leaders
Individuals who filter relevant information from operational variables into mission variables and execute the art and science of tactics.

PMESII-PT
An acronym for the eight operational variables used to analyze an operational environment: political, military, economic, social, information, infrastructure, physical environment, and time.

Defense Support of Civil Authorities
One of the four elements of decisive action.

Mission Variables
Categories derived from operational variables used by Army leaders during mission analysis to understand the context of their missions.<SEP>Factors that determine the optimal size and mix of capabilities of the forces task-organized under a division headquarters.

Army Planners
Individuals who use operational variables to analyze and describe an operational environment.

Army Doctrinal Hierarchy
A framework introduced in the publication that organizes the content, subordinate publications, warfighting functions, and defeat mechanisms.

Decisive Action
A framework consisting of four elements: offense, defense, stability, and defense support of civil authorities.

Stability
One of the four elements of decisive action, often conducted alongside other elements.<SEP>A condition or objective relating to the reestablishment or maintenance of order within a region or host nation.

Warfighting Functions
Groups of tasks and systems united by a common purpose that commanders use to accomplish missions and training objectives.

Tactical Mission Tasks
Tasks that describe both actions and purposes, possessing specific military definitions distinct from common English.

Defeat Mechanisms
Mechanisms organized within the Army doctrinal hierarchy, mentioned alongside warfighting functions.

JP 3-0
A joint publication that defines the twelve principles of joint operations and provides guidance for military operations.<SEP>JP 3-0 is a joint publication that established joint functions and provides definitions for areas of influence, interest, and operations.<SEP>A publication defining economy of force.<SEP>A joint publication referenced as the source for the definition of maneuver.<SEP>JP 3-0 is a joint publication referenced regarding the definition of a joint special operations area.

Military Decision-Making Process
A critical process during which the analysis of mission variables is conducted.

Figure 2-1
A figure illustrating the taxonomy of the Army’s tactical doctrine for the four elements of decisive action and tactical mission tasks.

data.content:
Field Service Regulations United States Army
A publication from 1923 where the principles of war (now joint principles) were first published in America.

Tacticians
Individuals who apply common tactical concepts, military definitions, and echelons to conduct offensive and defensive operations.

Large-Scale Combat Operations
A type of operation during which units performing close combat are unlikely to conduct stability tasks.

Economy Of Force
A principle of war where commanders employ measures to expend minimum essential combat power on shaping operations to support the decisive operation.

Engagement Area
A designated area where a commander intends to contain and destroy an enemy force with the massed effects of all available weapons.

Encirclement Operations
Operations where a force loses freedom of maneuver because an opposing force isolates it by controlling all ground lines of communications.<SEP>Military operations where a force loses freedom of maneuver because an opposing force isolates it by controlling all ground lines of communication.

Unified Action
The operational context in which Army forces apply land power as members of an interdependent joint force.<SEP>Unified Action is supported by a special operations joint task force for special operations conducted in support of a campaign.

JP-1
A joint publication referenced for additional information on joint interdependence.

Combat Power
Combat power consists of warfighting functions, leadership, and information, used by commanders to accomplish missions.<SEP>Power generated by a force, which can be concentrated overwhelmingly against separate enemy elements in defeat in detail.<SEP>The military capability that commanders manage, expending minimum amounts on shaping operations to provide maximum power for decisive operations.<SEP>Combat power is concentrated on enemy vulnerabilities and demonstrated through the rapid reaction of the regiment.

Enemy Force
The opposing military entity that friendly forces seek to destroy, isolate, or gain advantage over during operations.

Flank
The right or left limit of a unit, designated by enemy location for stationary units or direction of movement for moving units.

Assailable Flank
A flank exposed to attack or envelopment due to terrain, force weakness, technical capability of an opponent, or gaps between units.

Ground Lines Of Communication
Routes used for supply and reinforcement, the control of which allows a force to isolate an opponent during encirclement operations.

Forms Of Contact
The eight categories of military contact: visual, direct, indirect, non-hostile, obstacles, aircraft, CBRN, and electronic.

Flanking Position
A geographical location on the flank of a force from which effective fires can be placed on that flank.

Local Security
Low-level security activities conducted near a unit to prevent surprise by the enemy and provide immediate protection.

Position Of Advantage
A location or favorable condition within the area of operations providing temporary freedom of action to enhance combat power over an enemy.

CBRN
Chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear warfare, identified as one of the eight forms of contact.

FM 3-90-2
A field manual referenced for further information on encirclement operations.

Direct Fire
Fire activities inherent in maneuver and close combat.<SEP>Gunfire directed at a target visible to the aimer, which a unit cannot concentrate as effectively on its flanks as it can to the front.

Electronic Contact
A form of contact that includes contact in cyberspace.

Intelligence Warfighting Function
The intelligence warfighting function comprises related tasks and systems that facilitate understanding the enemy, terrain, weather, and civil considerations.

Stability Tasks
Stability tasks are activities that units are unlikely to conduct if they are also performing close combat in large-scale combat operations.

Cyberspace
A domain within the information environment where electronic contact can occur.<SEP>Digital domain used as a means for disseminating psychological operations products.

Warfighting Function
A warfighting function is a group of tasks and systems united by a common purpose that commanders use to accomplish missions and training objectives.<SEP>A Warfighting Function is a capability that alone does not generate sufficient power to prevail, requiring integration via combined arms.

Command and Control Warfighting Function
The command and control warfighting function consists of related tasks and systems that enable commanders to synchronize and converge all elements of combat power.

Movement and Maneuver Warfighting Function
The movement and maneuver warfighting function involves related tasks and systems that move and employ forces to achieve a position of relative advantage over the enemy.

Information
Information is an element of combat power alongside warfighting functions and leadership.

Protection Warfighting Function
The protection warfighting function involves related tasks and systems that preserve the force so the commander can apply maximum combat power.

Fires Warfighting Function
The fires warfighting function includes related tasks and systems that create and converge effects in all domains against the adversary.

Defeat Mechanism
A defeat mechanism is a method through which friendly forces accomplish their mission against enemy opposition.

Isolate
Isolate is one of the four defeat mechanisms used by tactical forces.

Sustainment Warfighting Function
The sustainment warfighting function consists of related tasks and systems that provide support and services to ensure freedom of action and extend operational reach.

Leadership
Leadership is an element of combat power alongside warfighting functions and information.

Area of Influence
An area of influence is a geographical area wherein a commander is directly capable of influencing operations by maneuver or fire support.

Destroy
Destroy is one of the four defeat mechanisms used by tactical forces.

Dislocate
Dislocate is one of the four defeat mechanisms used by tactical forces.

Disintegrate
Disintegrate is one of the four defeat mechanisms used by tactical forces.

Close Combat
Combat activities inherent in maneuver, involving direct fire, which units are unlikely to conduct alongside stability tasks.

Terrain
A physical aspect of the operational environment understood through the intelligence warfighting function.<SEP>A physical factor that affects cross-country mobility, supporting range, and the tactical mobility of different unit types.

Area of Interest
An area of interest is an area of concern to the commander, including the area of influence and areas adjacent thereto, extending into enemy territory.

Joint Functions
Functions established in JP 3-0 to which Army warfighting functions are linked.

Weather
A physical aspect of the operational environment understood through the intelligence warfighting function.<SEP>An environmental factor that affects cross-country mobility and can restrict the mobility of Army aviation units.

Tactical Forces
Forces at all echelons that use combinations of defeat mechanisms against enemy opposition.

Friendly Forces
Military units belonging to one's own side or allies, which security and fire support measures aim to protect.<SEP>Forces that accomplish their mission against enemy opposition using defeat mechanisms.

Operational Environment
The environment comprising enemy, terrain, weather, and civil considerations that the intelligence warfighting function facilitates understanding of.

Stability Mechanisms
Stability mechanisms are methods used in the conduct of stability operations.

Reserve
An uncommitted force withheld from action at the beginning of an engagement to be available for decisive movement.

Civil Considerations
Aspects of the operational environment understood through the intelligence warfighting function.

Domain
Realms or dimensions across which the fires warfighting function creates and converges effects.

A commander who assigns subordinate Areas of Operations for land and maritime forces.<SEP>A commander under whom a division normally operates with operational control.

A commander who assigns subordinate Areas of Operations.

A commander who assigns subordinate Areas of Operations.

Command levels that provide support for regeneration processes.

Standing Rules of Engagement
Established rules of engagement set by the Joint Chiefs of Staff, which operational-level commanders can modify.

Armored Ground Maneuver Units
Units such as combined arms battalions that possess good tactical mobility, firepower, and protection.

Weighting the Decisive Operation
A tactical concept associated with mass and maneuver principles, focused on the decisive operation.

Army Aviation Maneuver Units
Units with excellent mobility in most terrain but limited protection, restricted by extreme weather.

Rules of Engagement
Directives issued by competent military authority that delineate circumstances and limitations for initiating or continuing combat engagement.

Infantry Ground Maneuver Units
Units like airborne infantry battalions that have tactical mobility advantages in restrictive terrain but limited firepower.

Joint Chiefs of Staff
The body that has established standing rules of engagement.

Tactical Mobility
The ability of friendly forces to move and maneuver freely on the battlefield relative to the enemy.

Unit Self-Defense
The inherent right and obligation of unit commanders to exercise defense in response to a hostile act or intent.

United States Forces
The military forces governed by rules of engagement regarding the initiation and continuation of combat.

A field manual referenced for additional information on reconstitution.

Equipment used by units to engage targets, determining the supporting range and influencing rules of engagement.

Military units equipped with Stryker vehicles that possess good tactical mobility but less firepower and protection than armored forces.

Firepower
A combat power factor that defines tactical mobility and varies among different unit types such as armored and infantry.

Protection
A combat power factor that defines tactical mobility and varies among different unit types such as armored and infantry.

Cross-Country Mobility
A component of tactical mobility that is affected by terrain, soil conditions, and weather.

Military Members
Individuals who may exercise individual self-defense in response to hostile acts or intent.

JAGIC
Joint Air Ground Integration Center, a unit manned and equipped to control tactical airspace over a division area of operations.

Joint Airspace Control Plan
A plan developed with the participation of Army airspace planners to govern airspace control.

Army Airspace Planners
Personnel at senior operational and tactical levels who help develop the joint airspace control plan.

Individual Self-Defense
The right of military members to defend themselves in response to a hostile act or intent unless directed otherwise by a commander.

Airspace delegated by the airspace control authority to a division, located between the rear boundary and the FSCL.

An airspace coordinating measure using altitude to separate users and transition between different airspace control elements.

Control methods used throughout division-assigned airspace, primarily relied upon by the JAGIC.

Area Air Defense Commander
A commander retaining specific authorities not delegated to the division regarding airspace control.

Division AO
The Division Area of Operations over which a JAGIC-enabled division exercises procedural control.

Shadow
An unmanned aircraft for which the JAGIC acts as the airspace control agency during division deep operations.

Positive Control Methods
Control methods limited to areas controlled by Army or joint air traffic control elements.

Minimum-Essential Stability Tasks
Tasks related to providing civil security, food, water, shelter, and emergency medical treatment to civilians.<SEP>Essential tasks including providing civil security, food, water, shelter, and emergency medical treatment to civilians in accordance with laws of war.

Rotary-Wing Aircraft
Aircraft separated from fixed-wing aircraft by the coordination level procedural method.

Division Aviation Elements
Aviation units operating within the division area of operations, integrated by BCTs or JAGIC.

Brigade Combat Team responsible for airspace management within their area of operations and integrating division aviation elements.

A document that specifies control for division aircraft and the authority of brigades over unified action partner airspace users.

Gray Eagle
An unmanned aircraft for which the JAGIC acts as the airspace control agency during division deep operations.

Multifunctional Support Brigades
Brigades that conduct operations throughout a corps or division area of operations and coordinate airspace use.

A field manual referenced for information regarding orders annexes.<SEP>FM 6-0 defines liaison as contact or intercommunication maintained between elements of military forces.

An element that checks and adjusts the airspace plan to account for multifunctional support brigade priorities.

Fixed-Wing Aircraft
Aircraft that normally will not fly below the coordinating altitude, as determined by the coordination level.

A command whose aircraft may operate in division-assigned airspace and receive procedural control from the JAGIC.

Division Aircraft
Aircraft for which the airspace control appendix specifies control procedures.

A publication referenced for additional information on stability tasks.

Partners whose airspace users' authority varies and is specified in the higher echelon headquarters airspace control appendix.

A publication referenced for additional information on environmental considerations.

An element within a multifunctional support brigade that receives planning and airspace control support from higher echelon headquarters.

Civil Authorities
Designated government bodies, agencies, and organizations responsible for providing basic needs to people within a unit's area of operations.<SEP>Authorities responsible for providing the basic needs of people within a unit's area of operations.

Civil Security
A minimum-essential stability task provided to civilians located within a unit's area of operations.<SEP>Civil Security is one of the six primary stability tasks to be established by units.

Avenue of Approach
A path used by an attacking force leading to an objective or key terrain, existing in all domains.

Airspace Plan
A plan adjusted by the division airspace element to account for a commander's priorities and concept of operations.

Combined Arms
The integration of capabilities from joint, multinational, interagency, and other organizations where weapons and units operate together effectively.

Environmental Considerations
Factors that must be integrated into planning and operations by commanders, significantly affecting units consolidating gains or remaining in a location.

Key Terrain
Key Terrain is a tactical location that provides an advantage, mentioned as a destination for an avenue of approach or a position to be held in decisive engagements.<SEP>Key Terrain refers to strategic locations seized and secured by the 75th Ranger Regiment.

Committed Force
A force in contact with an enemy or deployed on a specific mission that precludes its employment elsewhere.

Economy of Force
The judicious employment and distribution of forces to allocate the maximum possible combat power on primary efforts.

Principle of War
Fundamental guidelines for conducting war, under which economy of force is categorized.

Decisive Engagement
An engagement where a unit is fully committed and cannot maneuver or extricate itself without outside assistance.

Attacking Force
A military force that uses an avenue of approach to maneuver towards an objective or key terrain.

Objective
An Objective is a goal or destination of an attacking force, reached via an avenue of approach.

Ground Lines of Communications
Routes used for supply and reinforcement, control of which allows an opposing force to isolate another force during encirclement operations.

Brigade Task Forces
Formed when brigades and BCTs task-organize by the attachment or detachment of outside organizations.

Civil Control
Civil Control is one of the six primary stability tasks to be established by units.

Essential Services
Essential Services are to be restored as one of the six primary stability tasks.

Governance
Governance is to be supported as one of the six primary stability tasks.

Economic and Infrastructure Development
Economic and Infrastructure Development is to be supported as one of the six primary stability tasks.

Opposing Force
An Opposing Force is a military entity that isolates another force by controlling ground lines of communications during encirclement operations.

Security Cooperation
Security Cooperation is one of the six primary stability tasks to be conducted by units.

Concept of Operations
A statement directing how subordinate units cooperate to accomplish a mission and the sequence of actions to achieve the end state.

Brigade Support Battalion
A unit normally contained in all types of Brigade Combat Teams.

Cavalry Squadron
A unit normally contained in all types of Brigade Combat Teams.

A field manual providing details on Brigade Combat Teams and their subordinate units.

A unit normally contained in all types of Brigade Combat Teams.

A unit normally contained in all types of Brigade Combat Teams.<SEP>A specific unit component within Special Forces Groups responsible for command and control.

160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment
One of the two tactical regiments currently retained by the Army.<SEP>A premier tactical unit conducting worldwide high-risk aviation operations and supporting joint force units with precision rotary-wing aviation.<SEP>The 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment conducts and supports special operations missions for various commands and can be task-organized based on mission requirements.<SEP>The 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment is the Army's special operations aviation unit supporting special operations.

75th Ranger Regiment
One of the two tactical regiments currently retained by the Army.<SEP>A direct reporting unit included within USASOC.<SEP>A unit receiving dedicated, mission-configured unmanned aircraft system support from the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment.<SEP>The 75th Ranger Regiment is a specially trained, rapidly deployable force that performs demanding missions in support of national and theater operational objectives.<SEP>The 75th Ranger Regiment is a conventional infantry unit specializing in complex offensive operations and participated in Operation JUST CAUSE.<SEP>The 75th Ranger Regiment is the Army's premier special operations infantry force capable of rapid deployment.

Regional Support Groups
A unit type that is an exception to the rule regarding deactivated group headquarters.

Military Police Corps
An Army branch containing a single regiment intended to perpetuate history and traditions.

Corps of Engineers
An Army branch containing a single regiment intended to perpetuate history and traditions.

Division Headquarters and Headquarters Battalion
The organization into which the Army organizes each division headquarters staff.

Groups
Brigade-size organizations rarely used outside of Army’s special operations forces.

Explosive Ordnance Disposal
A unit type that is an exception to the rule regarding deactivated group headquarters.

Criminal Investigation Division
A unit type that is an exception to the rule regarding deactivated group headquarters.

Army Special Operations Forces
Army Special Operations Forces constitute the Active and Reserve Component Army forces designated to conduct and support special operations within the Department of Defense. These forces are manned, trained, and supported by USASOC to execute missions aligned with theater and national objectives. The organization serves as a collective term for Army special operations units receiving logistical and aviation support to conduct missions, including Special Forces groups and battalions. Specifically, the forces use the term "Groups" to designate large special forces and psychological operations units. Within doctrinal contexts, the term serves as a contextual header for the employment considerations of Psychological Operations units within the Army.

Operationally, Army Special Operations Forces are deployed globally and operate under theater special operations commands. Their logistics support situational awareness is maintained by the 528th Sustainment Brigade, ensuring necessary support for worldwide deployments. Historically, these forces have engaged in diverse missions across different regions. Army Special Operations Forces personnel remained in Panama supporting stability operations and conducted various missions during Operation Just Cause. Additionally, between 2014 and 2022, forces assisted Ukraine with the development of laws, messaging, and defense capabilities.

A command to which Army forces may be assigned or attached.

Joint Special Operations Task Force
The Joint Special Operations Task Force is a task force formed to conduct special operations, composed of special operations forces from one or more Services or personnel from other United States Government departments and agencies. In certain contexts, it is established by Special Forces groups when augmented by other services, and potentially combines with United States Government departments or multinational SOF. The primary purpose of a Joint Special Operations Task Force is to control SOF assets and integrate special operations requirements.

The command and control architecture of the entity can be supplemented by special operations detachments. It may employ special operations command and control elements and provides liaison elements to facilitate operations. Functionally, the task force provides assets to augment an advanced operations base for specific mission sets. Within this operational framework, the 75th Ranger Regiment operates as a rapid response force subordinate to a Joint Special Operations Task Force, demonstrating the hierarchy and capability integration inherent to the organization.

FM 3-05
FM 3-05 is an Army Field Manual dated 26 June 2025 that serves as a comprehensive doctrinal document for Army Special Operations Forces. The manual outlines the organization, capabilities, and employment considerations of these forces, including specific information on regiment operations and the structure of special operations detachments within USASOC. Chapter 1 of the document addresses Army Special Operations Forces characteristics, while other sections detail the Command and Control structure essential for special operations forces.

The content extends to specific functional areas and units, providing information on Psychological Operations and the Civil Affairs brigade structure, capabilities, and employment considerations. Sustainment is also covered, with specific references to the 528th Sustainment Brigade and Army Special Operations Forces sustainment logistics. Additionally, FM 3-05 includes doctrine for Rangers and defines the roles of coordinating elements and liaison officers within the operational framework. This publication consolidates critical information regarding the command, control, and support structures necessary for effective special operations.
